reason: The claim drops the per-what of the 750 hours: the blog quote it cites for the date says '750 hours of public IPv4 address usage per month for the first 12 months', and the VPC guide quote gives no period at all, so a reader would take 750 hours as a total; the scope qualifier 'per account' is also in neither quote. The quotes do support the 750 hours at no charge for existing or new Free Tier customers with EC2, the charge outside the Free Tier, and the February 1, 2024 effective date.

Quote 1 under Internet gateway basics > Routing configuration defines public and private subnet by a route to an internet gateway in the associated route table; quote 2 states that without that route instances in the private subnet can't communicate with the internet even with public IP addresses. All three displays are verbatim.

The Gateways row under the Name | Default | Adjustable header gives Carrier gateways per VPC = 1 and Adjustable = No; a non-adjustable default is the maximum, so 'can have 1 carrier gateway, not adjustable' matches.

The Benefits bullet 'Higher port and IP limits' states up to 32 IP addresses per Availability Zone for regional NAT gateways, compared to 8 for zonal, and 55,000 more concurrent connections per IP address to a unique destination IP, port and protocol; the claim restates it with the same 'up to' and per-AZ scope.

Under How regional NAT gateways work, the two mode bullets state automatic mode (AWS manages IP addresses and AZ expansion, recommended) and manual mode (you are responsible for expanding and contracting across AZs), matching both values.

The Benefits bullets state a regional NAT gateway is a standalone resource with its own route table needing no public subnet, and a single NAT ID across all AZs that have network interfaces so subnets in different AZs use the same route entry; the intro quote repeats the no-public-subnet point.

The quote on Visualize the resources in your VPC states the resource map shows relationships inside a VPC and traffic flow from subnets to NAT gateways, internet gateway and gateway endpoints, word for word.

The Route Server page quote states it dynamically updates VPC and internet gateway route tables with preferred IPv4 or IPv6 routes for routing fault tolerance, and context adds automatic rerouting within a VPC; the Document history row dates the guide entry March 31, 2025, matching 'in the VPC guide since'.

Under Route priority for static and dynamically propagated routes the quote states that with identical destinations the static route takes priority; the claim keeps the identical-destination condition.

The 10.0.0.0/8 row of the restrictions table lists the other RFC 1918 ranges, the 10.0.0.0/15 versus 10.0.0.0/16 rule and 198.19.0.0/16 as restricted, and as permitted any other unrestricted 10.0.0.0/8 block, publicly routable blocks or 100.64.0.0/10 blocks, each between /16 and /28; the claim matches every part.

The feature page states Security Group VPC Associations associates a security group with multiple VPCs in the same Region and lets you manage it in one place for multiple VPCs in your account; the Document history row dates it October 30, 2024.

The page states sharing with other AWS Organizations accounts within the same Region so those accounts can use it, the requirements list states the sharing account must own both the VPC and the security group, and the Document history row dates it October 30, 2024.

The VPC size row of the Characteristic | IPv4 | IPv6 table states up to 5 CIDRs from /16 to /28 for IPv4 and up to 5 CIDRs from /44 to /60 in increments of /4 for IPv6, each with 'This quota is adjustable'.

Under Subnet sizing for IPv4 the quotes state the first four and last address are not available, list the five reserved addresses of 10.0.0.0/24, and give the roles of .1 (VPC router), .2 (reserved; DNS is base plus two), .3 (future use) and .255 (broadcast, not supported in a VPC), as claimed.

SEC05-BP01 implementation guidance states the data layer (databases, shared file systems) can reside in different private subnets from the application layer and that at each layer boundary you can deploy controls allowing only authorized traffic; the claim keeps 'can'.

The SEC05-BP03 statement says to set up traffic inspection points between network layers, and the implementation guidance states AWS Network Firewall and GWLB-based vendor solutions support different inline inspection deployment models.

The whitepaper Scalability section for centralized NAT egress states Transit Gateway generally does not act as a load balancer, would not distribute traffic evenly across NAT gateways in multiple AZs, and keeps traffic within an AZ if possible; the claim keeps 'generally' and 'if possible'.
